newsitem.title: USA: Richmond Fed's Broaddus -- US economy "favorable".
newsitem.headline: Richmond Fed's Broaddus -- US economy "favorable".

text.p: The current state of the U.S. economy remains favorable, but there is some inflation risk from rising price pressures, said Alfred Broaddus, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond.
"The state of the general economy is very, very favorable," Broaddus said at reception here sponsored by Christopher Newport University.
Labor markets are quite tight, but so far that has not boosted inflation, Broaddus said.
"Inflation has remained exceptionally subdued despite the tght labor markets," he said.
Productivity increases appear to be one factor offsetting wage-related inflation pressures, he said.
Discussing recent solid U.S. economic growth, Broaddus said the "wealth effect" of stock market gains has boosted consumer spending, the largest component of Gross Domestic Product.
But if the economy were to expand at or above 3.0 percent in 1997, the unemployment rate may dip toward 5.0 percent from its current 5.2 percent, he said.
"If we get that sort of performance, one of the main things we're concerned with at the Fed is, what does that imply for the rate of inflation," Broaddus said.
The recent rise in long-term interest rates suggests investors expect higher inflation rates in the future, Broaddus said, adding that the Fed expects only a modest increase in prices in 1997.
Broaddus said there were downside risks in the economy, noting that many households were extended with credit card and other kinds of consumer debt.

"There is a concern that if the economy were to weaken and job growth were to slow for whatever reason ... you could see households beginning to tighten up their spending on goods and services," he said.
But he also noted his own feeling was that "currently most of the risks in the outlook are on the upside ... with the possibility of rising inflationary pressures."
"There is not much head-room for further acceleration in growth," Broaddus said.
Broaddus listed a drop in health benefit costs, job insecurity and the strong dollar as factors keeping inflation subued, but said all these factors could be fleeting.
"The dollar strength has led many American business firms, especially in the manufacturing sector to be reluctant to raise prices for fear of being undercut by foreign competition," Broaddus said.
"It's possible the dollar will weaken over the course of this year ... and if that were to happen that would be another factor taking out this beneficial effect on inflation," he added.

Turning to the Fed's inflation-fighting mission, Broaddus acknowledged inflation sometimes improves at the cost of economic growth, but said no evidence supports a long-term inflation/growth tradeoff, he said.
Broaddus said that "stabilizing the price level essentially means getting rid of inflation, not tolerating over the long haul at least any inflation."

The Richmond Fed Bank President also said that Europe faces a "very, very difficult transition" in achieving its goal of economic and monetary union, but said he was optimistic about prospects for global economic growth.
Broaddus also stressed the importance of sensible fiscal policy as a prerequisite for sensible monetary policy.
((-- Noah Barkin & Scott Gerlach, N.A. Treasury Desk 212-859-1673))
